opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that they're complementary, and the interesting question is really about the trade-off between them for a given problem.

For a long time the field's mental model was that almost all the action was in training. You scale up the data, the parameters, and the compute you spend pre-training, and capability emerges. That's been enormously productive. But if you look at some of the work we've done at DeepMind, particularly in science and in areas like mathematics or algorithm discovery, a lot of the breakthroughs came from combining a strong learned model with substantial search or iteration at inference time. AlphaGo is the classic example: the network gives you intuition, but the search on top of it gives you the depth. And in systems where you can generate candidate solutions and then verify them, like proposing programs and checking them against an evaluator, spending more compute at inference time can unlock results the model alone simply wouldn't reach.

So the way I think about it is this: training-time compute builds intuition, a good prior over what's likely to work. Inference-time compute lets you explore, reason, and check. When you have a reliable verifier, whether it's a proof checker, a simulator, or a test suite, inference-time compute becomes extraordinarily valuable, because you can turn more thinking into more correctness. When you don't have a good verifier, you lean much more heavily on the quality of the prior, and therefore on training.

There's also a nice feedback loop between the two. The outputs of expensive inference-time search, once verified, become excellent training data. So you can distill what the system discovered through search back into the model, and the next generation starts from a stronger intuition. That's something we've seen pay off repeatedly.

From a practical standpoint, there's an economic dimension too. Training compute is a one-time investment amortized over every use of the model, whereas inference compute is paid every time. So for problems where a single answer is enormously valuable, say discovering a new material or a better algorithm that runs on billions of machines, it makes total sense to spend a huge amount at inference time. For everyday queries, you want as much capability baked in as possible.

So I wouldn't say one matters more than the other. The frontier is really about learning how to allocate between them intelligently, and ideally building systems that can decide for themselves how hard to think about a given problem.

r001.rationale: The response says training-time and inference-time compute are complementary and explicitly says neither matters more than the other.

r002.rationale: It says verified search outputs can be distilled into training data, giving the next model stronger intuition, but does not identify improved internal representations as a mechanism for better prediction.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the framing of inference-time versus training-time compute as a competition is a bit misleading. They're really complementary, and the interesting question is how they interact.

Let me explain how I think about it. Training-time compute is about building a good prior. You're compressing a huge amount of experience into the weights of a model, and that gives you a system that can produce reasonable answers very quickly. But there's a limit to what you can get from the prior alone, because the model is essentially pattern-matching against what it has already seen. For a lot of problems, especially ones that require reasoning, planning, or verification, the right answer isn't something you can just retrieve. You have to search for it.

That's where inference-time compute comes in. Search is a very old idea in AI, and we've known for a long time that a weak model with a lot of search can beat a strong model with no search. AlphaGo is the obvious example. The policy network on its own was decent, but combined with Monte Carlo tree search it became superhuman. And what's happening now with reasoning models is really a version of that same lesson. You let the model think longer, explore multiple paths, check its own work, and you get a much better answer than you would from a single forward pass.

But here's the part people sometimes miss. The two aren't independent, because what you learn at inference time can be fed back into training. If the model does a lot of search and finds a better solution, you can distill that into the weights, and now the prior is better, so the next round of search starts from a higher point. That's the loop that made AlphaZero work, and I think it's the loop that's going to matter most going forward. Training-time compute improves the prior, inference-time compute exploits the prior and discovers things beyond it, and then you close the loop.

The other thing I'd say is that the economics are different. Training compute is paid once, inference compute is paid every time you use the model. So for problems where you need a fast answer, or where you're serving billions of queries, you want as much as possible baked into the weights. But for hard problems, a mathematical proof, a scientific hypothesis, a complex piece of code, spending a lot of compute at inference time is clearly worth it. You wouldn't expect a mathematician to solve a hard problem in a second, so why would you expect a model to.

So I don't think of it as one being more important than the other. I think the real frontier is in how much you can get out of the interaction between them, and in being smart about when to spend compute where, depending on the problem in front of you.

r001.rationale: The response says training-time and inference-time compute are complementary and that neither is more important overall.

r002.rationale: It says distillation improves the model’s prior, but does not identify improved internal representations as the mechanism for better prediction.

astra-6.text:
I think both are important, and they play complementary roles. Training is where the model develops the capabilities that it can then bring to a problem. Inference-time compute gives it an opportunity to use those capabilities more effectively—to explore different solutions, check its work, and revise an answer.

One useful analogy is the distinction between answering a question immediately and spending some time thinking about it. Extra time can make a big difference, especially for a difficult reasoning problem. But thinking longer only helps if you have useful ways to make progress. So the quality of the training still matters enormously.

The interesting question is how we train models to make productive use of that additional computation. Can they recognize when a problem needs more thought? Can they verify a candidate solution? And can they stop when further computation is unlikely to help? I see training-time and inference-time compute as increasingly connected, rather than as competing approaches.

r001.rationale: The response says training-time and inference-time compute are both important and complementary, and emphasizes that training quality matters enormously.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention distillation or improved internal representations as a prediction mechanism.

sol-6.1.text:
I think both are important, and they play complementary roles. Training is where the model develops capabilities and learns useful representations. Inference is where it applies those capabilities to a particular problem, and giving it more time to reason, explore alternatives, or check its work can make a substantial difference.

But more inference-time compute doesn’t automatically give you a better answer. The model needs to have learned how to use that compute productively. Can it identify a mistake? Can it verify a candidate solution? In mathematics or coding, where you can often check an answer, that creates a powerful opportunity.

So I wouldn’t frame it as choosing one over the other. The interesting question is how we train models that can make effective use of additional computation at inference time—and judge when a problem needs that extra effort.

r001.rationale: The response says training and inference are both important and play complementary roles in improving models.
